p: Of all the conquerors in history, Alexander of Macedon is the one whom historians find hardest to judge, because he did so much so young, and died before we could see what he would make of it. He became king at twenty. In the eleven years that followed, he conquered the Persian Empire, the greatest state the world had yet seen, marched his army from Greece to Egypt and from Egypt to the borders of India, and founded more than a dozen cities bearing his own name. He died in Babylon at thirty-two. Whether he was a visionary who wished to unite mankind, or a brilliant and increasingly drunken young man who simply could not stop fighting, has been argued since antiquity. The evidence permits both views, which is perhaps why both have flourished.

Macedon was a kingdom to the north of Greece proper, whose people the southern Greeks regarded as half-barbarian: they spoke a dialect hard to understand, they had kings, they drank their wine unmixed with water, and they were very good at fighting. Alexander's father, Philip the Second, made the Macedonian army the finest in the world, armed with pikes so long that a block of men holding them presented an impenetrable hedge of points, and with a heavy cavalry of noblemen, the Companions, who rode beside the king. With this army Philip subdued the Greek cities, defeating Athens and Thebes at the battle of Chaeronea in three hundred and thirty-eight years before Christ, and was preparing to invade Persia when he was murdered at his daughter's wedding, in three hundred and thirty-six.

Alexander had been educated by Aristotle, the greatest philosopher of the age, which is perhaps the most striking meeting of pupil and teacher in history. What Aristotle made of his pupil's subsequent career, we do not know; he had told him, it is said, to treat the Greeks as friends and the barbarians as beasts, and Alexander, to his credit, did not take the advice.

In three hundred and thirty-four, Alexander crossed into Asia with some thirty-seven thousand men. He beat the Persian satraps, or governors, at the river Granicus, and then the Persian king himself, Darius the Third, at Issus, in what is now the south of Turkey. He besieged the island city of Tyre for seven months, joining it to the mainland by a causeway, and when it fell he crucified, so the ancient writers say, two thousand of its men. He was welcomed in Egypt as a liberator from the Persians, and visited the oracle of the god Ammon in the desert at Siwa, where the priest is said to have greeted him as the son of the god. Alexander seems to have believed it, or found it useful to be believed. At Gaugamela, in three hundred and thirty-one, he defeated Darius a second time and decisively. Darius fled and was murdered by his own nobles. Alexander became King of Asia.

He did not stop. He marched into the mountains of what are now Afghanistan and the lands to the north, fought for three hard years against guerrilla resistance, married a local princess named Roxana, and in three hundred and twenty-six crossed into India, where he defeated a king named Porus, who fought with war elephants, at the river Hydaspes. There, at last, his army refused to go further. They had marched many thousands of miles in eight years; they wished to see their homes. Alexander sulked in his tent for three days, as Achilles had in the Iliad, which he carried with him and slept with under his pillow, and then gave way. On the return, he led part of his army through the Gedrosian desert, in the south of what is now Pakistan, where thousands died of thirst and heat. Two years later, in Babylon, after a long drinking bout, he fell ill with a fever and died, in June of three hundred and twenty-three. Asked, the story goes, to whom he left his empire, he answered: to the strongest.

His virtues were real. He was brave to the point of madness, always leading the charge, and he was wounded many times. He was generous, often merciful to the defeated, and capable of great charm. He tried, more than any Greek before him, to treat the Persians as partners rather than subjects, adopting Persian dress and court ceremony, enrolling Persian youths in his army, and at a great festival at Susa marrying himself and some ninety of his officers to Persian noblewomen. His Macedonians resented all this bitterly.

His vices were equally real. He grew suspicious and violent. He had several of his oldest officers executed on charges of conspiracy. In a drunken quarrel he killed with his own hand Cleitus, a friend who had saved his life at the Granicus. He destroyed the city of Thebes and sold its people into slavery, and burned the great palace of Persepolis, perhaps in revenge for the Persians' burning of Athens, perhaps merely in drink.

His empire did not survive him as a single state. His generals, called the Successors, fought for decades over it, and divided it into kingdoms: the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Asia, the Antigonids in Macedon. But it was in these kingdoms that the true consequence of his conquests appeared. For three centuries, until Rome absorbed them, Greek became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean and the Near East. Greek cities, Greek theatres, Greek gymnasiums and Greek philosophy spread as far as Afghanistan, where Greek kings later ruled and Greek sculptors helped to shape the first images of the Buddha. At Alexandria in Egypt, the city Alexander founded, the Ptolemies built the greatest library of the ancient world, where scholars edited Homer, measured the earth, and translated the Hebrew scriptures into Greek. That translation, made for the Jews of Alexandria who no longer read Hebrew, became the Bible of the early Christians; the New Testament itself was written in Greek. This age, which historians call the Hellenistic, from the Greek word for Greek, was in many ways the foundation of the Roman world and of Christianity. Alexander conquered for glory. He opened, without intending it, a door between East and West that has never quite been shut.
